name: Tiriyó
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Meira, Sérgio. 1999. A Grammar of Tiriyó. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston (UMI 9928570; hdl 1911/19417). §2.5 Prosody (p. 60), §2.5.1 Rhythmic stress, pp. 60-71 (§2.5.2 Intonation begins p. 71).
catalog_quote: The following rules summarize the various facts described above, giving an overall characterization of Tiriyó rhythmic stress in terms of (C)V ('light') or non-(C)V ('heavy') syllables. (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. [p. 63] ... Tiriyó phonological words follow a pattern of alternation between non-prominent (unstressed) and prominent (stressed) syllables. If the phonological word is composed exclusively of (C)V syllables, then every second syllable from the beginning of the word will be stressed, except for the last syllable, which is always unstressed. [p. 60] ... For the time being, aside from an impression that the last stressed syllable in a phonological word sounds stronger than the others, there seems to be no reason to analyze any single syllable in a phonological word as bearing primary stress. This conclusion may change when more is known about the phonetics of the Tiriyó stress system. [p. 71]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Trió is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's two items are one paper: Meira 1998 'Rhythmic Stress in Tiriyó (Cariban)', IJAL 64(4): 352-378, DOI 10.1086/466366 (Glottolog 93167 is a duplicate from Fabre's bibliography with the author wrongly given as Edmundo Magaña; Crossref confirms Meira). The article is paywalled and could not be downloaded (no OA copy per Semantic Scholar; publisher/JSTOR 403; not on archive.org/HathiTrust). Its analysis is available first-hand in Meira's open Rice dissertation (1999, hdl 1911/19417, already held by the project under salu1254 and now linked into trio1238), pages 60 and 63 read directly from renders: iambic rhythmic stress, final syllable never stressed, every non-final heavy syllable stressed, every second light syllable from the word start or the nearest heavy syllable stressed, no primary stress identified (p. 71), length not pitch as the cue (p. 70). Meira 2006 ELL2 (held by the project) repeats this as 'weight-sensitive rhythmic (iambic) stress' citing Meira 1998. Recommended catalog's classification for a new record: rhythmic/iambic, weight-sensitive, left-to-right, final extrametrical, no culminative primary stress. Still worth acquiring: Meira 1998 IJAL (high, paywalled) and Carlin 2004 A Grammar of Trio (print only) as an independent second description.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (page render of book p. 63 = p. 84 of the Rice dissertation symlinked from, 730 pp., UMI scan, no text). The passage is there verbatim: "The following rules summarize the various facts described above, giving an overall characterization of Tiriyó rhythmic stress in terms of (C)V ('light') or non-(C)V ('heavy') syllables. (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed." Rendered p. 92 (book p. 71) myself and read it on the image (saved): §2.5.1.4 "The question of primary stress. For the time being, aside from an impression…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iambic rhythmic stress computed left to right over the phonological word: in words made only of light (C)V syllables the 2nd, 4th, 6th.. syllables are stressed and the final syllable is always unstressed (so all-light monosyllables and bisyllables get no lengthened stress, only a pitch drop, pp. 66-67); every non-final heavy syllable (coda h/N, VV, VVh, VVN) is stressed and restarts the alternation after it. Stress shifts with prefixation (pakoro [pa.kó.ro] 'house' vs ji-pakoro [ji.pá.ko.ro] 'my house', p. 62). Phonetic cue is vowel length on stressed light syllables; pitch is intonational, not a stress correlate (p. 70). No culminative primary stress identified (p. 71).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction: all rhythmic stresses are treated as equal; Meira notes only an impression that the last stressed syllable sounds stronger (p. 71). Meira 1997 (Portuguese) calls all of them 'acento secundário'. Migliazza 1965 (older analysis) instead posits one phonemic primary stress per word plus a non-phonemic secondary stress one syllable away, primary usually on the 2nd syllable of 4-5 syllable words.
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllables never stressed; heavy syllables keep their stress regardless of position and reset the count; all-light bisyllables and monosyllables cannot form a foot (footnote citing Hayes 1995 extrametricality) and show only a pitch drop plus optional consonant lengthening; words with underlying long vowels (VV) keep length under affixation (p. 67). Migliazza 1965 p. 8 reports minimal pairs for stress (/e'pi/ 'remédio' vs /'epi/ 'lábio inferior dele') which Meira reanalyses as vowel-length (VV vs V) contrasts.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (Meira p. 60: 'rhythmic stress (with the phonological word as its domain)'); data are words pronounced in isolation, with intonation superimposed at utterance level (§2.5.2). Meira 1997 Bol. MPEG 13(2): 168 gives the same rule in Portuguese: 'acento secundário em todas as sílabas pares de uma palavra fonológica, contando-se da esquerda para a direita, com exceção da sílaba final, que nunca recebe acento'. Migliazza 1965 p. 8 (Portuguese, older, same Brazilian village) contradicts with a phonemic-stress analysis: 'Cada vocábulo tem um acento primário.. Os vocábulos de quatro ou de cinco sílabas, recebem, geralmente, o acento primário na segunda sílaba e o secundário na quarta.'
new_statements.identity_note: Meira 1999 (and Meira 1997, Migliazza 1965) describe the Brazilian Tiriyó of the Missão Tiriós villages on the upper Paru de Oeste (Pará); Meira's fieldwork also included Tëpu in Suriname. Carlin 2004 (not obtained) describes the Surinamese Trio. Same glottocode trio1238 throughout. Migliazza 1965 (same Brazilian village, 1960s) gives an older, divergent analysis (phonemic culminative primary stress) that Meira's rhythmic analysis supersedes.

sources.note: p. 8: 'O acento é fonêmico como o demonstram os seguintes pares mínimos: /e'pi/ remédio, /'epi/ lábio inferior dêle.. Cada vocábulo tem um acento primário /'/ e quando é constituído de três ou mais sílabas, pode ter um acento secundário [ ' ] não fonêmico.. Os vocábulos de quatro ou de cinco sílabas, recebem, geralmente, o acento primário na segunda sílaba e o secundário na quarta. Vocábulos de quatro sílabas, sendo a última de tipo V, recebem o acento na penúltima.' p. 12 English summary: 'Stress is phonemic.. Words consist of one to five syllables and have a phonemic primary stress.' Older…

sources.note: p. 168 'O sistema de acento rítmico do Tiriyó': secondary (rhythmic) accent on all even syllables of the phonological word counting left to right, except the final syllable, which never receives accent; valid without restriction for words of open syllables; non-CV syllables (CVh, CVN, CV:, CV1V2(N,h)) obligatorily accented and restart the pattern (p. 170); bisyllables/monosyllables left unresolved (fn. 3). Read on the page scan.
